deliverables.text: A labeled drawing of the settlement network as a weighted graph -- every vertex from Appendix A's node list and every edge with its fee weight written on it -- plus an explicit identification of at least one cycle in the graph, and a sentence stating what that cycle means for Fernbrook's settlement options.

A shortest-path determination: compute the total weighted cost of both candidate paths between the Issuing Bank (IB) and the Custodian (CU), show the arithmetic for each, and state which path is mathematically the shortest and why.

An Euler-audit determination: using the degree of every vertex in Appendix A's graph, determine whether the settlement network graph has an Euler circuit, an Euler path, or neither, and justify by counting each vertex's degree.

An expected-net-revenue-retained table comparing Option A (The Card Bridge's path) and Option B (The Coin Rail's path): total weighted path fee, expected fraud/dispute loss, and net revenue retained per $1,000 processed for each, shown step by step.

A one-paragraph written recommendation, using correct graph-theory vocabulary (vertex, edge, path, weighted graph, cycle) throughout, that names which rail retains more net revenue per $1,000 processed and explicitly addresses why comparing raw per-transaction fee percentages alone, without weighting each rail's real expected fraud-loss exposure, would have been misleading.

appendices.title: The Card Bridge: Fee & Dispute-Recovery Data
The Coin Rail: Fee & Fraud-Exposure Data

balance.argument_a: The Card Bridge's case rests on real recourse: two of its three edge weights are real, sourced, HIGH/MEDIUM-confidence published Visa figures [S1]/[S2] (1.89% + $0.10 interchange, 0.14% assessment), and the chargeback/dispute-resolution process genuinely recovers most of a disputed charge's value for Fernbrook (modeled at 80% recovered, MA1) -- a real, structural protection the Coin Rail definitionally cannot offer. A's expected fraud/dispute loss (0.18% of volume) is small precisely because that protection exists. A's weakness is arithmetic, not principle: at Fernbrook's small $1.30 average transaction size, the interchange rate's flat $0.10 component becomes a very large proportional cost (roughly 7.7% of the transaction on its own), and that flat-fee drag is the single biggest reason A's total cost load is nearly six times B's under this case's own numbers.
balance.argument_b: The Coin Rail's raw fees are genuinely tiny -- a $0.01 flat network fee and a 0.05% off-ramp fee, versus the Card Bridge's 2.03% + $0.10 -- and that gap is real, not exaggerated. Its real, structural weakness is total, not partial, loss exposure: with zero dispute recourse, every fraud/dispute event costs Fernbrook the full transaction value, versus only 20% of it under the Card Bridge. Even after weighting that full exposure at the case's stated 0.90% fraud-incidence assumption (MA4), the Coin Rail's expected loss (0.90% of volume) is five times the Card Bridge's (0.18%) -- but the underlying fee gap is still large enough that B retains more net revenue per $1,000 processed. B's genuine case is that the raw-fee advantage survives properly weighting the real fraud exposure; it does not evaporate the way a shallow 'no chargebacks = risky, don't do it' reaction would assume.
balance.margin_basis: margin = 100 x |net_revenue(winner) - net_revenue(loser)| / net_revenue(loser), where net_revenue(option) = 1000 x (1 - total_fee_pct(option) - expected_loss_pct(option)) - total_flat_fee(option), and total_flat_fee(option) = (1000 / avg_txn_value) x flat_fee_per_txn(option) (the corpus's standard margin formula, per skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py -- loser is the denominator). Card Bridge (A): path IB-CN-AQ-MB, total_fee_pct = 0.14% + 1.89% = 2.03% [S1,S2]; flat fee $0.10/txn at $1.30/txn = (1000/1.30) x 0.10 = $76.92 per $1,000; expected_loss_pct = 0.90% (MA4) x 20% (MA1) = 0.18%. net_revenue(A) = 1000 x (1 - 0.0203 - 0.0018) - 76.92 = 1000 x 0.9779 - 76.92 = 977.90 - 76.92 = $900.98. Coin Rail (B): path AW-ST-CU-MB, total_fee_pct = 0.05% [MA, informed by S6]; flat fee $0.01/txn at $1.30/txn = (1000/1.30) x 0.01 = $7.69 per $1,000; expected_loss_pct = 0.90% (MA4) x 100% (definitional) = 0.90%. net_revenue(B) = 1000 x (1 - 0.0005 - 0.0090) - 7.69 = 1000 x 0.9905 - 7.69 = 990.50 - 7.69 = $982.81. margin = 100 x |982.81 - 900.98| / 900.98 = 100 x 81.83 / 900.98 = 9.08%, within the approved concept's 8-15% margin target. NOTE: only S1 (Visa interchange) and S5 (Base network fee) are used as real sourced numeric edge weights directly in this arithmetic; S2 (Visa assessment) is a real but aggregator-sourced MEDIUM figure; MA1 (dispute-recovery share), MA2 (unused pilot edge), MA3 (avg transaction value), and MA4 (fraud-incidence probability) are all stated Modeling Assumptions -- this margin is a designed property of those assumptions' chosen values, not a pure empirical finding.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Merchant-borne loss share of a disputed transaction on the Card Bridge (chargeback/dispute-recovery process)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes an exact merchant-borne loss share for one specific dispute-resolution configuration -- this depends on authentication method, card brand rules, and processor tooling. Set well below 100% to reflect that card-network liability-shift and dispute tools genuinely recover most of a disputed charge's value for a merchant in good standing, while still leaving some fraud genuinely uncollectable even with recourse.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tested at +/-50% via sensitivity_model.py: does not flip the verdict (margin moves only from 9.0% to 9.2%) -- this dial turns out to matter far less to the recommendation than MA3 or MA4 do, because it only scales the Card Bridge's already-small expected-loss term.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source discloses a per-transaction rate for this specific, real, publicly announced pilot (a card network settling to a stablecoin custodian instead of a traditional acquirer). Set between the near-zero pure on-chain rate and the full card interchange rate, reflecting hybrid infrastructure cost.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change which option wins in this case's current numbers -- this edge is not part of either option's actual path, only the network map, cycle check, and Euler-audit deliverables.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes Fernbrook's own transaction sizes (a fictional company). Set low and disclosed, consistent with real 2026 industry reporting (Appendix F, S7) that AI-agent-initiated payments run frequent, small-value transactions specifically because a flat per-transaction fee becomes proportionally large at small transaction sizes even when the percentage fee stays modest.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tested at +/-50% via sensitivity_model.py: moves the margin substantially (6.3% at +50% up to 18.3% at -50%) but does not flip the verdict in either direction -- the Coin Rail's fee advantage is large enough to survive a halving or 50% increase of the average transaction size, even though how CLOSE the race is changes a great deal.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Probability a given reorder-agent transaction becomes a fraud/dispute event
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source measures a fraud/dispute incidence rate specific to AI-agent-initiated, card-not-present micro-transactions. Informed by two real, cited findings: the Nilson Report's worldwide blended card fraud rate of 6.58 cents per $100 (0.0658%) for 2023 [S3], and the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City's finding that card-not-present fraud rates are meaningfully higher than card-present rates and rising [S4]. Since every transaction in this case is card-not-present by construction, 0.90% is set roughly an order of magnitude above the blanket all-card-types aggregate to reflect a card-not-present-only channel, without multiplying it several orders of magnitude beyond what the cited data would support.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tested at +/-50% via sensitivity_model.py: margin moves from 8.7% (+50%, fraud more common) to 9.5% (-50%, fraud less common) but does not flip the verdict -- the Coin Rail's raw fee advantage at this case's $1.30 transaction size is large enough that even a 50% swing in the fraud-incidence assumption does not overcome it, though it remains the single dial with no direct public benchmark behind it.
